headline: Gold struggling above $4,000 USD due to strong inverse correlation with the USD and high cost of carry versus bonds and equities; recovery contingent on dollar turning or equity risk aversion returning
reasoning: Barratt observes that gold is currently trading almost purely as a function of the US dollar's strength, with the inverse correlation very strong. The high cost of holding gold (opportunity cost relative to high-yielding US bonds and a Nasdaq at record highs) is discouraging investment. He argues gold will regain favour only if the dollar weakens or equity market concerns emerge. Silver is also flagged in the same context. At present gold is described as a 'poorer cousin' to other asset classes.
quote: Look, when you put the price of gold, overlay it with the US dollar, you get a sense of that. Inverse correlation is very, very strong at the moment. So so gold is just really trading on the fact that its cost to hold is a lot higher. And as a result of that cost, people saying, well, look, I can switch out and I can go into bonds, I can go into something else. Remember, the Nasdaq is on record highs for some reason. Again. Um, you know, and people are saying, well, let's rotate out of this because it's costing me money and gold hasn't performed as a result of that. If the dollar turns around, if people see there are concerns in equities, then gold will regain favor. But at the moment, um, yeah. It's a poorer cousin to. To what? What else is out there.

headline: Oil flows through Strait of Hormuz recovering to ~98% of pre-war levels, making markets complacent but one geopolitical flare could reverse the easing
reasoning: Barratt notes that oil prices have eased partly due to strategic reserve releases and partly because markets are becoming comfortable that tanker flows through the Strait of Hormuz are back near pre-war levels (~98%). He flags that Houthi rebels are also retreating in Yemen, reducing another chokepoint risk. However, he cautions that markets are getting complacent and a single geopolitical incident could push prices sharply higher. The US sending a third carrier to the Middle East and Trump's threat to hit Iran in November add to residual upside risk.
quote: I think it has I think it's got to do with that also. I've got to it's also got to do with the markets getting comfortable that we're getting flows of oil through the Straits of Hormuz and pre-war levels. So the markets saying well, the players have given up a little bit in sort of pushing and shoving each other. And as a result of that, they're getting complacent. In fact, we're up to about 98% of pre-war flows. So that ensures that we're getting the supply through. So it is quite interesting because we are under a lot of pressure, and all it takes is just one little fire of something. And I think we go back up.

headline: Diesel crack spreads easing from peaks as Saudi Arabia adds supply and USD strength contains prices; domestic pump price relief likely if trend holds
reasoning: Barratt says diesel crack spreads, while still well bid, are starting to ease after peaking. Saudi Arabia has signalled additional supply into the market. The strong US dollar is also acting as a containing factor by reducing demand-side pressure and pulling the crack spread lower. He expects this to translate into relief at the petrol pump in Australia, noting the government has flagged 90 days of supply buffer, though elevated prices remain an inflationary concern given high RBA interest rates.
quote: I think that that is that it is starting to wheeze a little bit. They're still remaining quite well bid on the diesel side. But I think as we get that release of diesel and I think Saudi Arabia came out and said they're going to push more supply into the market as well. But when I look at the crack spread, I still think all it's all starting to ease. We're not seeing it as high. We obviously did peak up around that 1998, but at the moment she is coming back and and I think once again, that's that's getting relief into the market. The other thing I think which is really interesting too, is the value of the US dollar and the US dollar being quite well bit also playing into this mix as well.

headline: Still sees upside risk to Brent crude to US$100+, with Middle East conflict unresolved and no sign of de-escalation
reasoning: Barratt notes that despite renewed conflict between the US and Iran, tankers are not being disrupted in a concrete way, but supply risks remain elevated. He acknowledges that a global economic slowdown could dampen demand and cap prices, but overall believes the lack of concrete evidence of de-escalation keeps upside risk alive. He can see Brent crude trading with a US$100 handle or higher given current supply issues.
quote: I think that's the scary thing because we're seeing inaction but more conflict. Um, we're not seeing the tankers go through. Um, you know, the only good thing that occur is that the economics of things, economics of the globe could taper off and not be as bullish what people think. But I do think we still have supply issues there. And I still think that the price, given the lack of concrete evidence that the conflict is de-escalating, suggests that there is still risk to the top side. So I think I can still see a handle of US 100 on this, maybe even higher.

reasoning: Jonathan Barratt argues that silver remains in a structural supply deficit as it is not directly mined but comes as a by-product of other ores. Demand from China for solar panels and electric vehicles is driving imports of silver-bearing ore up 62% over the last two quarters. Silver previously rallied to US$120 before correcting sharply, but Barratt views this as a correction within an 'ultra bull market' rather than a trend reversal. He believes all the original demand drivers remain intact and that silver has the ability to reach US$100 and potentially beyond.

And when you look at the demand for silver, particularly out of China, for the likes of solar panels, electric cars, China is the lead. headline: Bullish on wheat: 11% weekly and 30% since June rally likely to continue, driven by converging super El Niño weather risk, Ukraine/Russia Black Sea export disruption, and constrained alternative supply routes
reasoning: Wheat has rallied 11% in the past week and 30% since end of June. Multiple supply-side pressures are converging: a predicted super El Niño threatening both Australian and US Great Plains production, ongoing conflict reducing Ukrainian exports from Black Sea ports, and limited alternative routing via the Danube with its tonnage constraints. World ending stocks are not at a comfortable buffer level and could be drawn down quickly, which would cause further price hikes and feed through to inflation and CPI. The combination of weather risk and geopolitical supply disruption creates a strong bullish case.
quote: You've got, you know, the the Black Sea, you've got the exports of, of wheat from there, Russia and Ukraine. So it's just not one area. There's multiple areas which are conforming to make this a good bullish argument... if the Super El Nino or the largest record on record has that effect. Then we're going to see a significant drop in production. And that to me is one of the major concerns... people still consuming prices are still there. And this is a staple, staple stable product staple product. So if you get that you don't get that supply you're ending. Stocks will sort of reduce very quickly. And as a result of that you'll see continual price hikes, which of course in itself is a major component to inflation, CPI, etc.
